title: Topological classification through knotted graphs: Fermi surface dispersions and Lifshitz transitions
authors: Hakan Akgün, Xianquan Yan, Ching Hua Lee
abstract: Knot theory has provided a rich topological taxonomy for band structures, but its reach is fundamentally limited: knot invariants classify only 1D nodal lines at gap closure, and cannot encode the full dispersion or rich Fermi surface structure of realistic materials. Here we show that knotted graphs (knots that admit graph-like intersections in 3D space) - which have so far been elusive in condensed matter literature - provide a unified topological language for classifying the entire band dispersion, and even the eigenstate topology in some contexts. We propose a new framework beyond the existing Yamada polynomials that can topologically characterize the intricacies of realistic Fermi surfaces completely, crucially including how their multiple disconnected pieces are nested. This yields the Yamada set, a boundary-resolved extension which organizes the full topological evolution across energy into a Yamada sequence: a compact dispersion-level fingerprint directly tied to experimental signatures of Lifshitz transitions. Our framework is demonstrated with DFT-based band structures of real materials. Beyond dispersion-level classifications, this framework can be extended to non-Hermitian exceptional surfaces, where Berry-curvature flux further equips the knotted-graph skeleton with a directed Abelian edge flow that also captures the eigenstate topology.
summary: This work establishes a novel topological framework using 'knotted graphs' to classify the entire energy dispersion of electronic materials, moving beyond simple nodal line analysis. By defining the 'Yamada sequence,' the authors provide a robust, energy-dependent fingerprint that directly predicts Lifshitz transitions. This methodology is highly general, extending to characterize complex structures like intrinsic linkedness in exceptional surfaces.
main_problem: The paper aims to develop a unified topological language to classify the entire band dispersion and Fermi surface structure of realistic electronic materials, overcoming the limitations of traditional knot invariants.
main_result: The authors introduce the Yamada set and Yamada sequence, a boundary-resolved fingerprint that provides a global topological characterization of the full energy dispersion, directly linking to experimental signatures of Lifshitz transitions.
method: The method involves skeletonizing Fermi surfaces into knotted graphs and assigning a topological invariant, the Yamada polynomial, which is then tracked across energy levels to form the sequence.
model_or_system: The framework is applied to electronic materials, analyzing Fermi surfaces ($\Sigma$) derived from band structures, often illustrated using a two-component Hamiltonian $H(\mathbf{k}) = [	ext{Re } f(\mathbf{k})] \sigma_x + [	ext{Im } f(\mathbf{k})] \sigma_z$.
key_observables: The Yamada sequence (a compact dispersion-level fingerprint), the topology of the Fermi surface ($\Sigma$), and graph properties like planarity and intrinsic linkedness.
important_parameters: Fermi energy ($E$), Hamiltonian coefficients (e.g., $t_8$ in $	ext{Co}_2	ext{MnGa}$), and energy thresholds ($F_{min}, F_{max}$).
main_assumptions: The standard Yamada polynomial is insufficient for materials with multiple disconnected components or nested boundaries, necessitating the advanced boundary-resolved Yamada set.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the process: mapping Fermi surface evolution to knotted graphs, calculating the Yamada polynomial, and generating the sequence fingerprint across energy windows, with supplementary figures detailing planarity and intrinsic linkedness.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the limitations of existing invariants, proposes the knotted graph framework, details the boundary-resolved Yamada set, demonstrates its application to Fermi surface evolution across energy (Lifshitz transitions), and extends the analysis to intrinsic linkedness using graph minors.
why_interesting: While focused on solid-state topology, the rigorous mathematical machinery developed—using graph minors (Petersen graphs) to characterize intrinsic linkedness and developing a sequence fingerprint—provides powerful, generalizable tools for characterizing complex topological phases in quantum systems.
